title: Luke 5:1–11
context: Teaching by the Lake of Gennesaret, Jesus borrows Simon’s boat, then tells the tired fisherman to let down his nets again. The huge catch brings Simon to his knees: “Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, Lord.” Jesus answers, “Don’t be afraid,” and calls him to catch people. Simon, James, and John leave everything and follow. Arminian and Reformed readers share this picture of holiness, grace, and costly discipleship; they describe the call’s inner working differently.

verses.text: Now while the multitude pressed on him and heard the word of God, he was standing by the lake of Gennesaret.
verses.arminianNotes: The crowd presses in to hear the word of God. Arminian readers see real hunger for God’s word among ordinary people, and Jesus meets it by teaching openly to all.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Luke calls Jesus’ teaching the word of God. The scene sets up a call that comes through that word.

verses.text: He saw two boats standing by the lake, but the fishermen had gone out of them and were washing their nets.
verses.arminianNotes: The fishermen are washing their nets after a failed night. Arminian readers see Jesus meeting people in the middle of ordinary work and disappointment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the Lord entering daily life unannounced. The empty nets prepare for a display of His power.

verses.text: He entered into one of the boats, which was Simon’s, and asked him to put out a little from the land. He sat down and taught the multitudes from the boat.
verses.arminianNotes: Jesus asks Simon to push out and teaches from his boat. Arminian readers note that Jesus invites Simon’s cooperation before calling him, drawing him in step by step.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Jesus taking the initiative with Simon. Simon hears the teaching before he sees the sign.

verses.text: When he had finished speaking, he said to Simon, “Put out into the deep and let down your nets for a catch.”
verses.arminianNotes: “Put out into the deep and let down your nets.” Arminian readers see a command that calls for trust and obedience from an experienced fisherman.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Jesus’ word carrying authority over Simon’s own trade and expertise.

verses.text: Simon answered him, “Master, we worked all night and caught nothing; but at your word I will let down the net.”
verses.arminianNotes: “At your word I will let down the net.” Arminian readers see faith as obedient response to Jesus’ word despite doubt and fatigue.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see obedience grounded in Jesus’ word rather than in Simon’s expectations. Faith rests on who is speaking.

verses.text: When they had done this, they caught a great multitude of fish, and their net was breaking.
verses.arminianNotes: The catch is so great that their net begins to break. Arminian readers see abundant blessing following simple obedience, a sign that Jesus can do what human effort could not.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see a sign of Jesus’ lordship over creation. The miracle is less about fish than about revealing to Simon who is in his boat.

verses.text: They beckoned to their partners in the other boat, that they should come and help them. They came and filled both boats, so that they began to sink.
verses.arminianNotes: Partners come, and both boats fill until they begin to sink. Arminian readers note that the blessing overflows to others, a hint of the shared mission to come.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the overwhelming scale of the catch, beyond any natural explanation. God’s provision exceeds what the fishermen can even hold.

verses.text: But Simon Peter, when he saw it, fell down at Jesus’ knees, saying, “Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, Lord.”
verses.arminianNotes: “Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, Lord.” Arminian readers see conviction awakened by encounter with Jesus’ holiness. Grace brings people to honest self-awareness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the response of a sinner before divine holiness, compare Isaiah 6:5. The title shifts from Master to Lord.

verses.text: For he was amazed, and all who were with him, at the catch of fish which they had caught;
verses.arminianNotes: Simon and all with him are amazed at the catch. Arminian readers see awe as a doorway to deeper faith, as the disciples begin to sense who Jesus is.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see amazement that recognizes power beyond human ability. Luke shows awe turning into recognition of Jesus’ holiness.

verses.text: and so also were James and John, sons of Zebedee, who were partners with Simon. Jesus said to Simon, “Don’t be afraid. From now on you will be catching people alive.”
verses.arminianNotes: “Don’t be afraid. From now on you will be catching people alive.” Arminian readers see Jesus answering conviction with grace and a new vocation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Jesus’ gracious call that turns fear into mission. The phrase catching alive suggests rescue, not capture.

verses.text: When they had brought their boats to land, they left everything, and followed him.
verses.arminianNotes: They bring the boats to land, leave everything, and follow. Arminian readers see a wholehearted response to Jesus’ call, freely given at real cost.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the effect of Christ’s call: those He summons leave all to follow Him. The record catch is left behind, showing a new treasure has taken its place.
verses.keyContrast: Both see a real call and a real response. Arminian readers usually describe the response as a free choice enabled by grace. Reformed readers usually describe Christ’s call as effectual, bringing about the response it seeks.
